title: Experimental runtime sandbox: safety, benchmarking, and observability manual
author: Ava Martinez
content:
Overview
--------
This manual documents the Experimental Runtime Sandbox ("Sandbox") used by engineering to safely run kernel scheduling experiments, profiling campaigns, and microbenchmark families against production-like stacks without exposing customer traffic. The goal is to provide repeatable processes, safety checks, telemetry expectations, and benchmark recipes so experiments can be run with minimal risk and high signal quality.

Intended audience
- Runtime engineers running kernel or scheduling experiments
- SREs validating performance/operational impact
- Research/Applied ML teams onboarding model variants into experiments

Key principles
- Isolation: sandbox instances must not be able to reach production control planes or persist customer data.
- Observability parity: the sandbox must expose the same telemetry surfaces (traces, metrics, kernel counters) as production.
- Incremental blast radius: start tiny (1-2 nodes) and scale only after passing guardrails.
- Reproducibility: each experiment must include a reproducible workload definition and seed set.

Quick reference SLOs for Sandbox test runs
- Synthetic latency target (sample workload): p95 < 120ms, p99 < 300ms.
- Throughput stability: mean throughput drift < 8% over 30-minute window compared to baseline.
- Kernel error rate: GPU kernel launch failures < 0.01% per-minute.
- Resource leakage: no orphaned processes or pinned memory > 5 MB per minute after tear-down.

Sandbox environments and naming conventions
- dev-sbx-<engineer>-<yyyymmdd>-vN (short-lived, free-form experiments)
- qa-sbx-chaos-<id> (used by SRE for fault-injection tests)
- perf-sbx-<model>-<profile> (used for benchmarking/model variant comparison)

Environment creation checklist
1. Verify the experiment has an associated ticket and owner.
2. Create sandbox VPC with egress-only NAT; no peering to prod.
3. Provision GPU nodes from the sandbox pool with node labels: sandbox=true, owner=<owner>.
4. Ensure KMS keys used are test keys; do not reuse customer KMS material.
5. Deploy runtime under feature-flagged build and enable extra logging (TRACE=kernel,harness).
6. Confirm Prometheus and tracing collectors point to sandbox ingestion endpoints.

CLI snippets
- Create sandbox cluster: redwoodctl sandbox create --name perf-sbx-bert-20241015 --gpu-type a100 --nodes 2
- Deploy runtime: redwoodctl deploy runtime --cluster perf-sbx-bert-20241015 --image gcr.io/redwood/runtime:exp-kernel-20241015
- Start workload generator: ./sbx-loadgen --profile=chat_short --concurrency=16 --duration=1800s --seed=42

Experiment config example (YAML)
- name: kernel-waveform-test-1
  owner: @ava
  cluster: perf-sbx-bert-20241015
  model: bert-base-384k
  build: exp-kernel-20241015
  workload: chat_short
  telemetry: [metrics, traces, kernel_counters]

Telemetry and observability checklist
- Metrics: request_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), tokens_per_second, kernel_launch_errors, gpu_mem_free_bytes, kvcache_hit_rate.
- Traces: full request timeline including kernel dispatch spans and kernel_id annotation.
- Kernel counters: per-kernel CUDA duration, SM occupancy, warp-efficiency estimates, L2 cache misses.
- Logs: runtime.INFO and runtime.DEBUG logs shipped to sandbox logging bucket.
- Sampling guidance: for medium experiments (10k requests) sample 5% full traces; for small experiments (1k requests) sample 100% for triage.

Profiling playbook (how to collect high-signal profiles)
1. Baseline run: 10-minute steady-state run of the chosen workload with the current stable kernel. Collect metrics and a 1% trace-sample.
2. Instrumented run: enable kernel-level tracing and nvprof capture for 120s at the 5-minute mark.
3. Differential comparison: generate flamegraphs for both runs and diff by kernel name and sequence length bucket.
4. Hypothesis validation: if increased latency maps to specific kernels, run microbenchmarks that pin sequence length and batch shapes to reproduce.
5. Regression triage: if latency is > 15% vs baseline at p95, stop and move to incident-style runbook (section: Failed experiment escalation).

Microbenchmark recipes (recommended canonical workloads)
- chat_short: 1–4 tokens prompt, typical PLG latency-sensitive route; concurrency 8–32; sequence length 256.
- long_context: 1–8 tokens prompt with 16k context retrieval; concurrency 2–6; sequence length 8192.
- search-embeddings: batch-size 128, measure tokens/s and memory footprint.
- rerank-burst: bursty pattern, 100 requests over 10s, then idle 50s; used to test cold-start behaviors.

Kernel scheduling knobs to test (and safe ranges)
- preemption_granularity: [ms] allowed range 1–50ms. Start at 10ms.
- batch_slice_target_ms: 5–40ms. Lower values reduce p99 but lower throughput.
- cooperative_yield_backoff: 0.5–4 (multiplier). Use 1.0 baseline.
- kernel_credit_limit: integer per-tenant limit; recommended test values 1, 4, 8.

Table: safe test matrix (examples)
Name | Nodes | Concurrency | Duration | Safety gates
-----|-------|-------------|----------|-------------
mini-smoke | 1 | 4 | 10m | kernel_launch_errors < 0.01%
stability-run | 2 | 16 | 60m | throughput drift < 5%
stress-burst | 4 | 64 | 30m | p99 < 3x baseline or auto-abort

Release-style checklist for promoting changes from Sandbox to Canary
1. Confirm experiment reproducibility and attach baseline vs experiment artifacts (metrics, traces, profiles).
2. Create a change request including kernel binary hash, config diff, and expected impact matrix.
3. Run a 4-hour stability-run in sandbox and pass SLOs.
4. Run canary in isolated prod tenant with 0.1% traffic and close monitoring for 6 hours.
5. If canary passes, increment traffic via automated rollout with automated rollback threshold: p95 increase > 20% or error rate increase > 0.1%.

Runbook: failed experiment escalation (step-by-step)
1. Immediately stop experiment traffic (redwoodctl sandbox stop --name <name>).
2. Snapshot pods and kernel logs: redwoodctl logs collect --cluster <cluster> --since 15m --output /tmp/snapshot.tgz
3. If kernel_launch_errors > threshold, mark experiment "unsafe" and alert runtime-alerts@redwood.com.
4. Triage owners: runtime-oncall -> experimental-owner -> applied-ml.
5. Reproduce in a clean sandbox cluster; if reproducible, open a kernel regression bug with reproducer and attach nvprof output.

Known limitations and common pitfalls
- Telemetry skew: sandbox ingestion pipeline can introduce up to 2–4% metric distortion due to sampling; account for it during comparisons.
- NVProf overhead: nvprof captures can add 10–30% latency during capture windows — never run nvprof in production.
- Resource packing differences: sandbox GPU instances may have slightly different NUMA locality vs prod fleet; include NUMA annotation when comparing.

Safety primitives implemented in the Sandbox runtime
- admission-controller sandbox-enforcer: blocks any deployment that references production secrets or KMS ARNs.
- runtime-feature-flag: experiments must be deployed with runtime.env.EXPERIMENT_ID set.
- automated abort: sidecar monitors p95 and kernel errors; if thresholds exceeded, triggers teardown.

PromQL queries to use for dashboards
- p95 latency: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le))
- kernel errors per minute: sum(increase(kernel_launch_errors_total[1m]))
- kvcache hit rate: sum(rate(kvcache_hits_total[5m])) / sum(rate(kvcache_requests_total[5m]))

Post-experiment artifacts required
- workload definition (seeded generator config) as a checked-in yaml.
- raw metrics tarball (Prometheus scrape or pushgateway export).
- sampled traces (trace IDs list and span export).
- nvprof and flamegraph artifacts.
- experiment retrospective: short doc with conclusions and recommended next steps.

Ownership and contacts
- Sandbox environment owner: @ava (eng-serving-runtime).
- Runtime kernel owner: @rohan (eng-serving-runtime).
- SRE validation @emily (eng-sre).
- Security contact for sandbox network reviews: security-oncall@redwood.com

Appendix: sample experiment retrospective template
1. Title and owner
2. Purpose and hypothesis
3. Baseline vs experiment: key metrics (table)
4. Profiles: top 5 kernels by added latency
5. Reproducibility checklist
6. Decision and next steps

Example decision snippet
- Decision: Roll forward cooperative_yield_backoff=0.8 in staged canary.
- Rationale: 12% p95 improvement on chat_short, no increase in kernel errors over a 4-hour stability run.
- Rollout plan: 0.1% -> 1% -> 10% traffic increments with 6-hour observation windows.

Notes and references

- See profiling-playbook/telemetry-feedback-kernel-autotune-playbook-2026 for autotuning loops.

This manual should be updated whenever a new telemetry surface is added or sandbox safety primitives change. For editorial changes, reach out to the document owner (author listed above).
